newsitem.title: USA: Greene County, Ala., files Chapter 9 bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: Greene County, Ala., files Chapter 9 bankruptcy.

text.p: Alabama's Greene County has filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy and hopes to produce a plan of readjustment in November, attorneys for the county said Monday.
The poor, rural county's only outstanding debt is a series of general obligation warrants issued in 1991 to build a new courthouse, said Robert Shields, the county's special bankruptcy attorney.
About $1 million is still outstanding from the $1.2 million issue underwritten by Porter, White & Co Inc. The next debt service payment of about $85,000 is due in February, Shields said.
He said the warrants were not in default, but it was unclear whether the county could make the next debt service payment.

"I and the county attorneys will evaluate the financial condition, income and expenses. They're going to have to do some expense cutting, obviously and come up with a plan of reorganization or readjustment, which would be submitted to the creditors, including the warrant holders, for their approval," Shields said.
Records show 38 buyers for the warrants, however some are brokerages so it was unclear how many warrant holders there were.
"I don't know how they'll be treated under a (reorganization) plan at this time. They will have an opportunity to approve, vote for and object to the plan," Shields said.
The Chapter 9 petition was filed Sept 11 in the U.S Bankruptcy Court in Tuscaloosa and the county has 120 days from that date to file a reorganization plan.
Our goal is to file a plan some time in November. That may be optimistic," Shields said.
He declined to comment specifically on the county's revenues and obligations and county officials were not available for comment.
However, Shields said the bankruptcy was partly due to to the loss of tax revenues from a dog racing track that had closed.

"This is probably the poorest country in Alabama," Shields said. "Because of the decline of the track and other matters, it just simply got in such a bind that it couldn't meet its general obligations".
Mike Johnson, a municipal analyst for Sandler O'Neil & Partners, estimated the county's gross revenues were under $20 million annually, but did not know the extent of their liabilities.
He described their situation as "dire," but said, "It's not a dramatic implication for the bond market."

However, he said, "The question arises whether the county may have been quicker to pull the trigger on a bankruptcy filing because of Orange County's (Calif.) relatively painless experience with bankruptcy.

"Greene County moved to bankruptcy rather quickly," he said. "It's so rare until recently." the possiblity of municipal bankruptcy, especially in states like Alabama that have not historically intervened in local fiscal crisis.
Neither Moody's Investors Service Inc nor Standard & Poor's Corp rated the warrant issue.
